newsitem.title: USA: House to vote on Medicare plan with savings account.
newsitem.headline: House to vote on Medicare plan with savings account.

text.p: House lawmakers begin voting this week on a Republican Medicare plan that includes tax-free medical savings accounts the White House claims would undermine the medical insurance program for the elderly, aides said Monday.
Under a balanced budget deal reached by President Clinton and Congress, lawmakers must craft legislation to cut Medicare spending by $115 billion over five years.

The Republican bill, largely modeled on the budget agreement, includes a slight increase in Medicare premiums. The bulk of savings -- roughly $100 billion -- would come from cutting payments to doctors, hospitals and managed care plans.

While the medical savings accounts are controversial, many of the spending cuts in the plan are supported by the White House and congressional Democrats. A House Ways and Means subcommittee is expected to approve the bill this week.
President Clinton will meet with a bipartisan group of lawmakers Tuesday to discuss the emerging proposal.

Republicans included a medical savings account (MSA) proposal in their failed 1995 budget plan. The MSAs are similar to individual retirement accounts. They are used in conjunction with high-deductible catastrophic insurance plans that kick in for medical emergencies.

Under the Republican bill, Medicare recipients who opted for MSAs would be given a set amount of money to be deposited in a tax-free savings account. Funds could be withdrawn for routine medical bills. Any money left over at the end of the year could be rolled over to the next year.

Republicans say the proposal will make seniors more cost-conscious health shoppers. The administration is concerned the youngest, healthiest Medicare recipients will opt for the plan -- leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular Medicare program and increasing costs.

The Republican plan follows the budget deal in regard to Medicare premiums. It freezes the Part B premium for doctors' care at the current 25 percent of costs, rather than letting it fall as allowed under current law. Recipients also would pay about $4.50 per month more in higher premiums.

Medicare recipients would be allowed to choose from a wider array of health care plans. Doctors and hospitals would be given new power to band together to form their own health care networks. States would regulate the plans, but the federal government could waive state regulations.

The Medicare payment to hospitals would be frozen next year and lowered from the current reimbursement level in following years, according to industry officials. The plan also changes the payment rate for hospital outpatient care.
